On March 24, 2026, the ED team managed a difficult airway case involving a 58-year-old male MVA patient with facial trauma and suspected C-spine injury. The patient required emergent intubation with GCS 8, but significant challenges were encountered due to limited neck mobility, poor oropharyngeal visualization, and equipment limitations with our current video laryngoscope.

The case required three intubation attempts over 8 minutes, ultimately successful with bougie assistance. While the clinical outcome was favorable, the M&M conference review on March 26 identified critical equipment deficiencies that compromised optimal patient care.
Following the M&M conference, an equipment evaluation committee was formed to assess video laryngoscope options. The evaluation considered:

items: Image quality and screen visibility in ED lighting conditions
Blade variety and availability for diverse patient populations
Long-term cost analysis (initial purchase + maintenance/consumables)
Training requirements for resident education
Clinical performance in difficult airway scenarios
Budget constraints (target range ¥40,000-50,000)

blocks.text: **Option A: GlideScope AVL (Verathon)** - ¥45,000 initial cost, reusable blades, excellent optics, minimal maintenance (¥3,000/year). Five-year total cost: ¥60,000.
**Option B: McGrath MAC (Medtronic) newer model** - ¥38,000 initial cost, disposable blades (¥180 each, ~140 difficult airways/year = ¥25,000 annually). Five-year total cost: ¥138,000.
**Option C: King Vision (Ambu)** - ¥32,000 initial cost, but inferior image quality and limited blade options. Not recommended for high-acuity ED environment.
The decision was finalized in the ed-general Mattermost channel on March 31, 2026, following comprehensive evaluation and stakeholder input. Key discussion points included:

items: Dr. Wang Li recommended GlideScope based on previous institutional experience and superior clinical performance
Anesthesia department consultation confirmed GlideScope as gold standard for difficult airways
Resident feedback indicated both GlideScope and McGrath were acceptable, with slight ergonomic preference for GlideScope
Cost-benefit analysis strongly favored GlideScope over 5-year lifecycle (¥78,000 savings vs McGrath)
Equipment durability and reusable blade system reduce long-term operational costs

blocks.text: **APPROVED: GlideScope AVL Video Laryngoscope System with Reusable Blades (Adult Set)**

**Rationale**: The GlideScope AVL offers the best combination of clinical performance, long-term cost-effectiveness, and educational value for our high-acuity ED environment. Superior optics and blade durability address the specific equipment limitations identified in the March 24 difficult airway case.

title: Integrated Case Summary - Septic Shock M&M with Whiteboard Analysis

blocks.text: Comprehensive Case Review - Septic Shock Management
This integrated summary combines formal M&M conference notes (March 26, 2026) with clinical reasoning pathways and teaching frameworks captured on whiteboard during the session.
The whiteboard analysis revealed a detailed decision tree for septic shock recognition:

items: Initial triage assessment: SIRS criteria vs qSOFA score comparison
Differential diagnosis framework: septic shock vs cardiogenic shock vs hypovolemic shock
Time-sensitive intervention checklist: blood cultures → antibiotics → fluid bolus → vasopressors
Lactate trend interpretation: initial 6.2 mmol/L → 4.8 at 3h → 2.1 at 6h (clearance >30%)
Source control decision points: imaging timing, surgical consultation triggers

blocks.text: Whiteboard flowchart documented systematic approach to ruling out alternative diagnoses:

items: Hypotension + fever → Check for infection source (CXR showed RLL infiltrate)
Elevated lactate → Assess tissue perfusion (capillary refill >3s, mottled skin)
Mental status change → Rule out primary neurological cause (CT head negative)
Tachycardia out of proportion → Consider PE (Wells score low, no further workup)
Refractory hypotension → Early vasopressor initiation (norepinephrine started hour 2)

blocks.text: Teaching Points Not in Formal Minutes
The following insights were visible only in whiteboard photos and represent critical learning opportunities for residents:

items: Visual timeline of interventions showing actual vs ideal timing (blood cultures delayed 15 min due to difficult access)
Antibiotic selection rationale: local antibiogram showing 85% sensitivity to piperacillin-tazobactam for CAP
Fluid responsiveness assessment technique: passive leg raise test documented with hemodynamic parameters
Common pitfalls highlighted: over-resuscitation risk in elderly patients with heart failure history
Disposition decision framework: ICU admission criteria checklist with this patient's scores

title: M&M Conference - 床号23 Sepsis Case Presentation - April 8, 2026

properties.teaching_focus: Lactate clearance, fluid responsiveness, protocol compliance

blocks.text: 67-year-old male presenting with suspected intra-abdominal sepsis (likely cholecystitis source). Case demonstrates excellent sepsis recognition and protocol adherence with important teaching points about lactate trend interpretation and real-world documentation challenges.

items: 00:15 - Initial triage: BP 88/52, HR 118, Temp 38.9°C, Lactate 4.2 mmol/L
00:22 - Blood cultures obtained (sepsis alert activated)
00:28 - Broad-spectrum antibiotics ordered (ceftriaxone + metronidazole)
00:32 - Fluid resuscitation initiated (30ml/kg bolus)
00:47 - Antibiotics administered (19-minute delay from order)
00:58 - First fluid bolus completed, reassessment: BP 102/65, HR 106
01:30 - Lactate #2: 3.8 mmol/L (9.5% decrease)
02:15 - Clinical decision: Hold additional fluid bolus, continue monitoring
03:00 - Lactate #3: 3.1 mmol/L (continued improvement)
06:00 - Lactate #4: 2.2 mmol/L, patient clinically stable

blocks.text: Rapid sepsis recognition based on SIRS criteria + suspected infection source. Immediate activation of sepsis protocol with parallel interventions: cultures, antibiotics, fluid resuscitation. Initial lactate of 4.2 mmol/L confirmed tissue hypoperfusion and guided resuscitation intensity.

After initial 30ml/kg bolus, patient demonstrated clear fluid responsiveness: MAP improved from 54 to 68 mmHg, HR decreased from 118 to 106. Decision point at 02:15 - despite lactate still elevated at 3.8, clinical improvement and downward trend supported conservative approach rather than additional aggressive fluid loading. This clinical judgment was validated by continued improvement over subsequent hours.

Key teaching point: Gradual lactate clearance (not rapid normalization) is acceptable and often expected with adequate source control and resuscitation. This case demonstrated steady clearance: 4.2 → 3.8 → 3.1 → 2.2 mmol/L over 6 hours. The pattern, combined with improving clinical parameters, indicated effective resuscitation without need for escalation to vasopressors or additional fluid.

items: Rapid sepsis recognition and alert activation (<10 minutes)
Timely blood culture collection before antibiotics
Appropriate initial fluid resuscitation (30ml/kg)
Serial lactate monitoring per protocol (q1.5-3h)
Strong clinical assessment and decision-making
Antibiotic administration delay: 19 minutes from order to administration (pharmacy preparation + nursing workload factors)
Documentation timing gaps: 3-5 minute lag between actual intervention and documentation during high-acuity resuscitation
Action items: ED antibiotic stock protocol discussion with pharmacy, real-time documentation workflow review
Lactate trend interpretation: Focus on trajectory and clinical correlation, not just absolute values
Fluid responsiveness assessment: Integrate hemodynamic parameters, clinical exam, and lab trends
Protocol compliance in real-world practice: Understanding gaps between ideal protocol and clinical reality
Documentation challenges during resuscitation: Balancing real-time care with accurate record-keeping
Clinical judgment when labs improving but not normalized: When to hold vs. escalate therapy

blocks.text: Quality review committee agreed this case represents strong clinical care with minor protocol compliance gaps that reflect systemic challenges (pharmacy workflow, documentation timing) rather than clinical decision-making deficits. Case selected for M&M conference due to excellent teaching value around lactate interpretation and real-world protocol implementation.
